ru: проникаться симпатией, проникнуться (к кому-л.); одобрять, одобрить (идею)
separable: inseparable — what you take to follows *to*: *cotton to the idea*, never ✗ *cotton the idea to*.
gloss: To take a liking to someone, or to warm to an idea.
examples: The neighbors never *cottoned to* the new fence.
He does not *cotton to* being told what to do.
Investors have not *cottoned to* the idea at all.
contrast: Informal and a little folksy, and it turns up most often in the negative: *she didn't cotton to him*. British English has *cotton on to* for something else entirely — to finally understand — which Americans say as *catch on*.

ru: идти в минус, быть минусом; вредить, повредить (при оценке)
separable: inseparable — the person it hurts follows *against*: *counted against him*, never ✗ *counted him against*.
gloss: To be treated as a mark against someone who is being judged.
examples: A gap in your résumé should not *count against* you.
The late payments *counted against* her loan application.
Two missed shifts have already *counted against* his review.
contrast: The opposite is *count for*: *volunteer work counts for a lot here*. *Count against* is about an official judgment; *hold against* is about a personal grudge: *she still holds it against me*.

separable: no object — intransitive; the place follows the whole phrase: *crashed out on the couch*.
gloss: To fall asleep suddenly from exhaustion, usually not in your own bed.
examples: He *crashed out* on the couch with his shoes still on.
I will *crash out* the second we get back to the hotel.
Half the crew was *crashing out* in the van between shoots.
contrast: Informal. Plain *crash* does the same work — *I crashed at nine* — and *crash at someone's place* means to sleep over there.

ru: ужинать вне дома, поужинать в ресторане
separable: no object — intransitive; nothing comes between the two words.
gloss: To eat a meal at a restaurant instead of at home.
examples: They *dine out* twice a month, always on a Friday.
We *dined out* every night of the trip.
Families have been *dining out* less since prices went up.
contrast: *Eat out* is the everyday American phrase; *dine out* is a step more formal and belongs to restaurant writing more than to conversation.

separable: separable, and it must split — what you extract sits in the middle: *drag the truth out of him*, *drag it out of her*; ✗ *drag out of him the truth* is impossible.
gloss: To get information or an admission from someone who does not want to give it.
examples: It took an hour to *drag* the whole story *out of* him.
She *dragged* an apology *out of* her brother at the table.
I am tired of *dragging* answers *out of* that office.
contrast: *Pry out of* is the close cousin. Doubled consonant: *drag* → *dragged*, *dragging*.

separable: separable — *drum out the troublemakers* or *drum the troublemakers out*; with a pronoun it must split: *drummed him out*.
gloss: To force someone out of a group or a profession in disgrace.
examples: Two officers were *drummed out* of the department after the hearing.
The party is trying to *drum* her *out* before the convention.
They *drummed* him *out* for taking money from a contractor.
contrast: Almost always followed by *of* plus the group, and most often in the passive. Doubled consonant: *drum* → *drummed*, *drumming*.

ru: отделываться, отделаться (от кого-л. отговоркой); отфутболивать, отфутболить
separable: separable — the person goes in the middle: *fob him off*, *fob the customer off with a coupon*.
gloss: To get rid of someone by offering an excuse instead of real help.
examples: The airline *fobbed* us *off* with a ten-dollar meal voucher.
Do not let them *fob* you *off* again.
She has been *fobbed off* by three different departments.
contrast: Doubled consonant: *fob* → *fobbed*, *fobbing*. *Brush off* and *blow off* are the blunter American equivalents.

separable: separable — *fob off a fake* or *fob the fake off*; the buyer follows *on*: *fob it off on a tourist*.
gloss: To pass something worthless to someone by making it look better than it is.
examples: The dealer *fobbed off* a rebuilt engine as new.
He tried to *fob* the broken mower *off* on his neighbor.
Counterfeits are being *fobbed off* on collectors online.
contrast: *Palm off* is the more common American wording for this sense: *palmed off a copy as the original*.

separable: separable — *fork out the deposit* and *fork it out*; with no object it takes *for*: *fork out for a new roof*.
transitivity: both — transitive (*fork out four hundred dollars*), intransitive (*fork out for a new roof*)
gloss: To pay money for something, usually more than you would like to.
examples: We *forked out* almost two thousand dollars for that repair.
He will *fork* it *out* eventually, but he will grumble for a week.
Her parents have been *forking out* for tuition since September.
contrast: *Fork over* and *fork up* mean the same thing; *fork over* is the one you hear most in the US and the usual choice when the money goes straight to a person: *fork it over*.

separable: inseparable — it usually stands alone (*a neighbor happened by*), and a place can follow the whole phrase: *happened by the shop*, never ✗ *happened the shop by*.
transitivity: both — intransitive (*a neighbor happened by*), transitive (*she happened by the office*)
gloss: To come to a place by chance rather than by plan.
examples: Dad *happened by* just as we were loading the truck.
If you *happen by* before six, the door is open.
She has *happened by* twice this week with eggs from her hens.
contrast: Informal and warm. *Stop by* and *drop by* are planned visits; *happen by* is pure chance.

ru: натыкаться, наткнуться (на что-л.); случайно находить, найти
separable: inseparable — what you find follows *on*: *happened on a diner*, never ✗ *happened a diner on*.
gloss: To find or meet something by chance.
examples: We *happened on* a diner that was still serving pie at midnight.
You sometimes *happen on* a good bookstore that way.
He had *happened on* the letters while clearing out the attic.
contrast: *Happen upon* is the same phrase in a more formal register; *come across* and *run into* are the everyday American equivalents.

ru: восходить (к чему-л.), напоминать о прошлом; возвращаться, вернуться (к прежнему)
separable: inseparable — no object; what it recalls follows *to*: *harks back to the fifties*.
gloss: To bring to mind or deliberately imitate something from an earlier time.
examples: Designs like this *hark back* to the company's first delivery trucks.
His speech *harked back* to the strikes of the thirties.
Every episode keeps *harking back* to that first summer.
contrast: *Harken back* and *hearken back* are common American variants, but *hark back* is the standard spelling. The phrase is fixed with *to*, never ✗ *hark back on*.

separable: no object — a fixed run-up to a second verb: *hauled off and hit him*; nothing comes between the two words.
gloss: To draw back suddenly and then hit or lash out at someone.
examples: He *hauled off* and punched the guy in the parking lot.
If you *haul off* and yell at her now, you will lose her for good.
She had *hauled off* and slapped him before anyone could move.
contrast: Almost always *haul off and* plus a second verb, and that verb is sudden or violent. Used literally, *haul off* just means to cart something away: *the city hauled off the wreck*.

ru: запрыгивать, запрыгнуть (в машину); быстро забираться, забраться
separable: inseparable — what you get into follows the phrase: *hop into the car*, never ✗ *hop the car into*; with no object it is simply *hop in*.
gloss: To get into a car, a bed, or a shower quickly and without ceremony.
examples: *Hop into* the back seat — there is more room there.
She *hopped into* the shower before anyone else was up.
He was already *hopping into* his truck when I called after him.
contrast: Doubled consonant: *hop* → *hopped*, *hopping*. No jumping is involved — *hop into the car* just means get in, quickly.

separable: no object — what you intrude on follows *on*: *horn in on the deal*, never ✗ *horn the deal in*.
gloss: To push your way into something that is none of your business.
examples: A bigger firm is trying to *horn in* on our contract.
Her cousin *horned in* on the business after the first good year.
He has a habit of *horning in* whenever there is money involved.
contrast: Informal and disapproving. *Butt in* is the everyday equivalent for conversations; *horn in* is more often about a deal or a share of the money.
